item.title: Israeli Strikes in Gaza Kill Teenager and Civil Defense Worker, Local Official Says
item.description:
Israeli airstrikes in a residential Gaza neighborhood on Tuesday killed a teenager and a civil defense worker, according to a local official, amid mounting international pressure on Israel to halt its attacks in the enclave.

The Israeli military said that it had “directed an attack against Hamas terrorists” and that the outcome in the Gaza City attack was “under review.” The Israeli operation in Gaza followed strikes in the past day that the military said had killed Hamas militants.

On Tuesday, an Israeli drone strike in the Sheikh Radwan neighborhood of Gaza City killed a teenager, identified as Mohammed al-Zinati, 15, and wounded other people, a member of the civil defense team, Motaz Ayyoub, said in a phone interview.

A second drone strike less than a minute later killed Sharif Labad, a civil defense worker who was not on duty but had rushed to the scene, Mr. Ayyoub said. He said that he and Mr. Labad had been planning to meet and attend a wedding when his friend responded to the earlier strike.

“We are now in the mosque to do the funeral prayer,” Mr. Ayyoub said.

In separate statements on Tuesday, the Israeli military said that it had killed a Hamas commander in the northern Gaza Strip overnight and that it had killed two Hamas operatives on Monday, one in the Khan Younis area in southern Gaza and another in Gaza City.

Late on Tuesday, the Israeli military also said it struck “a senior Hamas terrorist” in the southern Gaza Strip. The office of Israel’s prime minister and minister of defense said in a joint statement that the strike had targeted the commander of Hamas’s Rafah Brigade and vowed that “Hamas will not remain in Gaza.”

Israel has continued to carry out deadly strikes in Gaza over the past six weeks, despite efforts by President Trump’s Board of Peace to halt the attacks following its announcement in late July that Hamas had agreed to surrender its weapons. Under the disarmament framework, Israel was expected to halt its military operations in Gaza except in cases of immediate self-defense, but Israeli officials rejected the agreement.

A senior Board of Peace official recently criticized Israel’s continuing strikes during a speech at the United Nations, saying that they did not serve Israeli interests and only delayed the demilitarization of Gaza.

The Israeli military operations in Gaza are taking place as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is campaigning for re-election and portraying himself as key to the country’s security. Jared Kushner, the Trump envoy and son-in-law who has been working with the Board of Peace on plans for Gaza, said earlier this month that Mr. Netanyahu’s government was acting “a little irrational” ahead of the election.

Volker Turk, the United Nations human rights chief, called on Tuesday for international investigators to be allowed into all parts of Gaza to recover the remains of Palestinians still buried under rubble, and to help gather evidence of potential war crimes.

He said in a statement on social media that remains believed to be from 96 people from three Palestinian families were recovered this month, including many women and children. Noting that Palestinian officials have estimated that thousands of people may still be buried under rubble, he said the findings so far “may only be the tip of the iceberg” because “much of Gaza has been flattened by Israeli bombing or demolition and clearing by heavy machinery and explosives.”

Doctors Without Borders said on Sunday said that one of its humanitarian vehicles was damaged and an aid worker injured when an Israeli strike in Gaza City targeted a vehicle less than seven feet away from them. The group said in a post on social media that the aid vehicle was clearly identified and accused Israeli forces of showing “a blatant disregard for the safety of humanitarian and medical personnel.”

“Nowhere is safe in Gaza,” Doctors Without Borders said, calling for civilians, health care workers and other humanitarian staff to be protected.

The Israeli military said in a statement that the attack in Gaza City on Sunday had targeted and killed two Hamas military wing operatives. The Israeli military said that it took steps to mitigate harm to civilians, including using “precise munitions and aerial surveillance.”

The Israeli military’s prosecution of the war in Gaza has come under further scrutiny in the past week after “NAZA,” a documentary about Palestinian civilian deaths in the war, premiered at the Venice International Film Festival. The Israeli directors received a 25-minute standing ovation and won the Special Jury Prize, but faced an official backlash at home.

The Israeli military chief, Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, consulted on Monday with top generals about how to respond to the film, saying it was based on “deliberate distortions of reality.”

On Tuesday, at a ceremony marking the start of the Jewish New Year, Maj. Gen. Yaniv Asor, who leads the military’s southern command, insisted on the importance of “maintaining the integrity of our own conduct, distinguishing between the enemy and those who are not involved in the hostilities.” He said this required the military to examine itself and “correct what must be corrected.”

But General Asor also said that Israeli forces would continue to operate in Gaza “to prevent Hamas from rebuilding its capabilities.”

item.title: Does the Stork’s Return to Britain Restore History or Rewrite It?
item.description:
The noisy throng of birds beat their wings and hopped up and down in their pen. These 3-month-old white storks, fueled by a generous morning’s feed, were ready for takeoff.

As a keeper twisted open the gate of the pen, a dedicated crowd of bird watchers in stork-themed shirts held its collective breath from several hundred feet away. The sight of a juvenile stork on its first flight is not to be missed.

The lanky bird, fabled in European folklore as a bringer of life, is now a permanent addition to Britain’s skies. It is also a surprisingly contentious one.

To the conservationists behind the yearslong effort to establish a population, the storks’ introduction restores a species that was presumed to have been wiped out in Britain some 600 years ago. To some more skeptical naturalists, it is a misguided act that introduces a bird that had never made Britain its home.

The White Stork Project, as the effort is known, has so far established a colony of some 100 birds at Knepp, a 3,500-acre former dairy farm in West Sussex.

Over two decades, the environment has done most of the reclamation there unaided as part of a wider “rewilding” effort that lets natural processes govern the landscape. But Isabella Tree, the conservationist who co-owns Knepp, is giving it something of a push with the storks.

Unlike other birds that could strike out and breed from just one pair, storks are a sociable species that are more likely to survive in a colony, she said.

To build that colony, conservationists have released captive-bred storks at Knepp every summer for the past eight years. The effort is working: Some 40 nests silhouette the landscape’s oak canopies.

This year’s batch of fledglings was bred at a zoo from flightless birds that had crashed into electrical pylons in Poland. After mingling with the colony’s existing population of wild-hatched chicks, the juveniles are embarking on a thousand-mile seasonal migration to northern Africa this fall. It is a grueling voyage: Most typically die in the attempt, but survivors will return three or four years later to find a mate.

Ms. Tree’s hope is that the colony will eventually become self-sufficient and spread across southern England to form satellite colonies. “We know that we can bring them back,” she said in an interview in July.

As the colony has grown, so has a re-examination of the archaeological and written record of its existence.

Though white storks have been spotted in Britain over the centuries, some researchers say there is little sign they made more than fleeting visits.

“We have no evidence from any source whatsoever that there were ever areas in Britain with a significant stork population,” said Ulrich Schmölcke, an archaeologist who specializes in birds at the Leibniz Center for Archaeology in Mainz, Germany.

By that logic, Knepp might be Britain’s first white stork colony ever.

The question has opened a ferocious debate over how actively conservationists should reshape the wilderness.

Archaeologists have unearthed the occasional adult white stork bone in Britain, but they have never found juvenile remains that would show the birds were not just visitors, Dr. Schmölcke said.

Nor do white storks appear in Britain’s rich canon of folk tales or written laws, he pointed out, as they do in parts of Europe where they are unquestionably native breeders.

The evidence, Dr. Schmölcke said, suggested “they never established a stable population.”

Ian Carter, an ornithologist who previously worked with the official environmental body Natural England, objected to the managed release of white storks on that basis. “No matter how many times people say it’s a ‘reintroduction,’ it absolutely isn’t,” he said.

The birds could pose a threat to existing wildlife, because they breed in high densities and prey on vulnerable wetland creatures, Mr. Carter said. “You can’t impose a species on the environment without having knock-on effects on other species,” he added. “And it changes the meaning of wildlife if you can just pick and choose any bird.”

The uproar prompted Natural England to weigh in with an assessment. In May, it said it had determined that white storks were never a native breeding bird.

Although the birds had visited from continental Europe, researchers could locate only a single historical reference to a nesting pair: In 1416, a Scottish priest observed two white storks building a nest on the roof of St Giles’ Cathedral in Edinburgh before they flew off. It was not clear from the text whether they bred successfully.

“It’s an animal that has turned up here sporadically,” said Tony Juniper, the chairman of Natural England. “But we can’t convince ourselves yet that this was an established species.”

While Mr. Juniper was effusive about the broader effort to “rewild” Knepp with native plants and other animals, he said the environmental authorities could not actively support the introduction of a species without an established breeding history in Britain.

In response to the skeptics, Ms. Tree said the standard of evidence they demanded — juvenile remains or legal records mentioning breeding — was impossibly high.

Storks were part of medieval Britain, she said, pointing to their appearance in artworks and place names. One is Storrington, a village near Knepp.

“Ultimately, you can argue either way,” Ms. Tree said. “And I don’t think it matters.”

The birds’ prominence as a symbol of fertility persists in cartoons and old-fashioned euphemisms about childbirth. A common theory for the link traces it to migration patterns: Storks would return to the skies of medieval Europe in February and March, coinciding with increases in human births around nine months after midsummer weddings.

Germanic mythology held that storks delivered the souls of newborn babies from subterranean lakes, said Ms. Tree, who is writing a book on the birds. In the early 19th century, the Danish writer Hans Christian Andersen adapted that idea in “The Storks,” a short story with a depiction of long-legged birds delivering newborns.

Bringing the birds to England has justifications beyond historical rectitude, Ms. Tree said. The storks’ large nests provide homes and food for other birds, she said. And the storks benefit from access to a cooler climate as continental Europe warms.

“We need to allow species to be able to move north in response to climate change,” she said.

While Ms. Tree’s critics contest her rationale, their objections are not a serious obstacle to her work. The releases at Knepp are independently funded and do not require official permission.

Mr. Juniper and Dr. Schmölcke both said that storks from mainland Europe could push north into Britain as the climate changes, regardless of the effort at Knepp.

At the estate in July, debates over their presence did not seem to concern the young storks as they took flight. Humans may have started the colony, but the birds did what feathered creatures tend to do. One by one they emerged from the pen, outstretched their wings and, after a few false starts, took flight.

Days later, the birds had embarked on their migration across the English Channel. Within weeks, some had been spotted in Morocco, scavenging in a garbage dump.

Jamie Craig, the zookeeper who had opened the pen to free the birds, responded with a resigned laugh to the image of them feasting on trash. “That’s life, that’s nature,” he said. “If we give it a resource, it will use it.”

item.title: A Corruption Case Spawns Memes and Indignation Among Ukrainians
item.description:
Ukrainians are used to revelations of corruption in their government. But one case that emerged this month has managed to grab their attention, in part because of a vivid turn of phrase.

An official working under Ukraine’s top prosecutor was caught on tape by anticorruption investigators describing his own approach to enriching himself through corruption.

“If you’re going to do something, then go all in — boom,” the official was recorded saying. He then explained, profanely, what he meant. If you’re going to sleep with a woman, he said, then sleep with “a queen.” And if you’re going to steal, then steal “a million.”

According to investigators, the official, Serhiy Kropyva, and others in the Office of the Prosecutor General did just that — the stealing part, anyway — through kickbacks they received for covering up a network of phone scammers working in Ukraine and abroad.

The allegations toppled the prosecutor general, Ruslan Kravchenko, who was formally removed from office on Tuesday by Parliament after President Volodymyr Zelensky called for his ouster. Mr. Kravchenko had already resigned last week.

He denies wrongdoing. He left Ukraine in recent days, saying that he was traveling abroad to discuss the work of anti-corruption bodies in Ukraine with partner countries — an explanation greeted with eye-rolls by his countrymen.

The official on the tape, Mr. Kropyva, has been arrested and is in pretrial detention. He at first denied that it was his voice but has since backed away from that claim. He says he is innocent of corruption.

The colorful recording has spawned memes as well as bitterness among Ukrainians. They have been sacrificing for their homeland, including through regular donations to the army, only to see an endless parade of officials accused of illicitly filling their own pockets.

Many Ukrainians see graft as a threat not only to the war effort but also to the country’s future. At the same time, they voice pride in the justice meted out in such cases, seeing it as a sign that the country’s democracy, including independent anti-corruption agencies, remains healthy after nearly five years of all-out war.

The scandal involving the Office of the Prosecutor General comes at a delicate moment for Mr. Zelensky, who has come under pressure to clean house amid the drip-drip-drip of corruption cases.

The revelations are especially stinging at a time when Ukraine is badly lacking money for the war. They threaten to sow doubts among the country’s European partners just as Ukraine asks for help in plugging its yawning budget gaps.

Russia has escalated attacks on the Ukrainian economy, striking warehouses, gas stations, railways and energy infrastructure with jet-powered drones for which Ukraine has not yet found an effective defense. The country’s prime minister, Serhii Koretskyi, said last week that Russian assaults would deprive the state of about $1.5 billion.

A clash over Ukraine’s anti-corruption efforts came to a head last year, when people took to the streets to safeguard the autonomy of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine, known as NABU, and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office. Both were created a decade ago with strong Western backing.

The Zelensky administration had moved to curb their power by placing them under the authority of the prosecutor general, who is approved by Parliament, where the president’s party holds a majority. Mr. Zelensky reversed course in the face of the demonstrations.

The prosecutor general who would have overseen the anti-corruption agencies was Mr. Kravchenko, the man who has now been felled in a corruption case.

Since the 2025 protests that preserved its independence, NABU has accused dozens of officials of corruption. The most highly publicized case, involving graft in the energy sector, led to the dismissal of Andriy Yermak, the powerful head of Mr. Zelensky’s office.

According to a survey conducted this summer by the Center for Social and Marketing Research in Kyiv, a majority of Ukrainians see corruption as having a stronger impact on the country than Russian bombings.

“These corruption scandals are terrible, and they are certainly demoralizing,” said Dmytro Kalach, 38, who works in light manufacturing and regularly donates money to the army.

He said that the graft would not deter him from continuing to support the military.

“The fact that they are scoundrels,” he said of government officials accused of corruption, “doesn’t mean I have to be a scoundrel like them.”

Some Ukrainians said they would carry on doing whatever it took to survive despite the corruption but still felt deeply hurt when cases came to light.

“I cannot simply shrug off these corruption scandals,” said Viacheslav Oksiuta, 68, a retiree from the military. He continues to work in the defense sector and is the father of two sons, one of whom is serving in the army.

“I can’t even watch television when I hear about these cases,” he said. “I take all of this very personally.”

Even as Parliament was taking action against Mr. Kravchenko this week, the drumbeat of corruption accusations carried on. Investigators said on Tuesday that they had discovered another illegal enrichment scheme, this time in a tax service office in western Ukraine.

item.title: The Canaduropean Union?
item.description:
President Trump has called Canada the 51st state, but will the country become instead the 28th state — of the European Union? The E.U.’s offer of an associate membership to Canada has prompted excitement and confusion in equal measure.

In January, Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada declared a “rupture in the world order” and called for middle powers to band together. I wondered at the time what he meant, and this might be part of it. But what would bringing Canada into the E.U. mean? What would it mean for Europe, whose geography as much as its values have always defined its borders, at least so far? And for Canada, whose own geography is the reason it’s been so dependent on the United States?

Today my colleagues Matina Stevis-Gridneff, who’s on the road with Carney, and Jeanna Smialek, who covers the E.U., write about the trickiness of inventing a new world order.

By Matina Stevis-Gridneff and Jeanna Smialek

To many observers, a tighter alliance between the European Union and Canada seems to make sense.

Trump has waged a relentless trade war with Canada, challenging its economy. The U.S. has also pulled back support for NATO and Ukraine, leaving the E.U. scrambling to shore up its defenses. That vacuum has left both Canada and the E.U. looking for new partners as the alliances established after World War II shift.

The invitation for Canada to become an “associate member” of the E.U., made yesterday by the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, shows just how intent these two traditional U.S. allies are on pursuing a stabler future by binding closer together. “We must urgently reimagine our partnerships,” von der Leyen said in a speech, as Carney sat next to her, beaming.

Between them, the E.U.’s 27 members and Canada have more than 490 million citizens, four of the world’s 10 largest economies, and a whole lot of desire to find partners outside the U.S. Carney often calls Canada “the most European non-European country.” E.U. leaders have spent years joking that it could join the bloc if only it were not on a far-flung landmass.

But yesterday’s announcement — which still falls well short of full membership — also highlighted the challenges involved in remaking the world order in real time. It may be easier said than done.

The 28th state?

The E.U. hinges on deep, dense legal and procedural rules, built over decades by a group of nations that ceded sovereignty to one another, and to an unelected executive branch in Brussels.

Bringing in a country an ocean away is not straightforward.

Canada does not actually qualify for full E.U. membership, since, ultimately, it’s not in Europe. But bringing it closer to the E.U. is still complicated. And the initiative began raising eyebrows within minutes of being announced on the floor of the European Parliament.

The issue was the name. The label the European Union wants to confer on Canada, “associate member,” is not an existing type of partnership. It has no obvious legal basis, and it’s not entirely clear what it would even entail.

The term has drawn consternation from several member states, who see it as vague, untethered from legal frameworks and potentially unfair to countries that already have detailed legal agreements with the E.U. That includes candidate nations such as Albania and also Britain and Norway, who have deep trade and defense ties to the bloc.

Some in Canada don’t appear to love it either. The Conservative opposition leader seized on the term, arguing that if Canada was to never be the 51st state of the U.S., it should also not become the 28th member state of the E.U.

Hours after von der Leyen spoke, the incoming Canadian ambassador to the E.U. said that Canada preferred “alliance for the future” to describe the emerging new bond with the E.U. “I think we’re still a ways away from actually landing on what we think the best way to describe it is,” he said.

Middle powers, acting together?

Ultimately, most experts agree the point is the symbolism.

In the run-up to the speech, European officials said the bloc did not want Trump to perceive Europe’s new energized partnership with Canada as an anti-American move.

This was “not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength,” von der Leyen said.

Still — if this isn’t a move against the United States, then it’s certainly about it.

Carney gave a headline-grabbing speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos this year. He argued that the world order that emerged from the Cold War was facing a “rupture, not a transition,” and that “middle powers must act together because if we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu.”

Yesterday’s announcement was a vivid demonstration of that strategy.

“It’s a big swing, politically and rhetorically,” said Jörn Fleck, a senior director focused on Europe at the Atlantic Council in Washington. “This is obviously signaling toward the U.S.” and “it’s also signaling to potential allies that the E.U. is willing to get more creative.”

Ed Sheeran’s world tour is in chaos over pro-Palestinian remarks made onstage by a supporting act, the rapper Macklemore.

Macklemore was removed from the tour this week, prompting four other supporting acts — Finneas, Aaron Rowe, the Danish pop band Lukas Graham and the Irish group Beoga — to quit the tour in protest. Each cited the need for free speech and voiced support for Palestinians.

Sheeran said the decision to remove Macklemore was made by the tour’s promoter and by the owners of the stadiums where concerts were booked. The next scheduled stop on Sheeran’s tour is in Philadelphia on Saturday.

The Turkish authorities are cracking down on L.G.B.T.Q. activists, saying it is an effort to protect families.

Belarus released 25 political prisoners after a U.S. envoy’s visit, signaling the growing ties between the countries.

As a candidate, Trump railed against forever wars. Now, he is desperate to avoid getting into one as the conflict in Iran drags on. David Sanger, our White House and national security correspondent, explains in the video below.

item.title: State Department Extends Visa Ban on Abbas, Other Palestinian Officials
item.description:
The State Department announced Wednesday that it would continue to deny visas to Palestinian officials because of actions taken by their governing and political groups that “internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian conflict,” including trying to bring cases to international tribunals.

The denial of visas would keep Mahmoud Abbas, the leader of the Palestine Liberation Organization and the Palestinian Authority, from attending the annual United Nations General Assembly in New York. The main part of that conclave starts next week.

This marks the second year in a row that the Trump administration has prevented Mr. Abbas from attending. In August 2025, weeks before the United Nations meeting that year, the State Department said Secretary of State Marco Rubio had decided not to issue visas to Palestinian officials in order to hold them “accountable for not complying with their commitments, and for undermining the prospects for peace.”

The State Department demanded at the time that the two Palestinian groups “consistently repudiate terrorism,” including the Hamas-led attack in Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and “end incitement to terrorism in education.” It also cited contacts between Palestinian officials and the International Criminal Court.

The Trump administration opposes Palestinians trying to bring cases to that court or the International Court of Justice.

About that time, the department also suspended issuing almost all types of visitor visas for anyone holding a Palestinian passport. That went well beyond earlier restrictions on visas of Palestinian visitors from Gaza.

The State Department said in a statement on Wednesday that it was extending the punitive visa measurements because the two Palestinian groups had not done enough to change their practices and were “glorifying terrorism.” The department said it had notified Congress of the visa ban extension.

item.title: Man Suspected of Shoving Woman in Front of Bus Is Found Dead, BBC Says
item.description:
A man who had been arrested on suspicion of shoving a woman in front of a moving bus in London in 2017 was found dead at his home on Tuesday, the BBC reported.

The Metropolitan Police said its officers had been called to an address in the West London neighborhood of Chiswick around 7 p.m. Tuesday after a 44-year-old man was found unresponsive at a house there. He was later pronounced dead, the police said, adding that the death was “unexpected but is not believed to be suspicious.”

The police did not name the man, but the BBC and multiple British news outlets identified him as Nicholas Brandram, 44, who was arrested in June in connection with the 2017 attack and had been released on bail. He had not been charged in the case.

According to the BBC, Mr. Brandram’s family said in a statement on Thursday that he “took his own life after months of immense pressure caused by a Metropolitan Police investigation” and there was “no credible evidence” linking him to the incident.

In May 2017, a male jogger, apparently unprovoked, shoved a 33-year-old woman in front of a bus as it was traveling along Putney Bridge in West London.

The woman fell backward and narrowly avoided serious injury when the bus driver abruptly swerved into the next lane, according to CCTV footage of the crime, which shocked Britain.

Surveillance cameras captured the jogger running on the other side of the bridge about 15 minutes later. He ignored the victim when she confronted him, video footage showed.

“The victim was put in extreme danger when she was knocked into the road,” Sgt. Mat Knowles, the investigating officer from the Putney Safer Neighborhoods Team, said in a statement after the attack. “It was only due to the superb quick reactions of the bus driver that she was not hit by the vehicle.”

At the time, the suspect, who came to be identified in the British news as the “Putney pusher,” was described only as a white man in his early to mid-30s, with short brown hair and brown eyes. The police looked into leads involving more than 50 people but said a year later that the trail had gone cold.

Nine years after the attack, the Met police said in June that they had arrested a 44-year-old man on suspicion of grievous bodily harm in relation to the incident. The police said last week that the man had been released. No charges had been brought.

Mr. Brandram was a former soldier in the British Army who more recently worked in private banking, according to the BBC.

item.title: Afghan Sentenced to 20 Years After Mixed Verdict in 2021 Kabul Attack Case
item.description:
An Afghan man was sentenced in Virginia on Wednesday to 20 years in prison in a case where prosecutors had sought to tie him to a suicide bombing outside the Kabul airport in 2021 but the jury delivered a mixed verdict.

The man, Mohammad Sharifullah, was found guilty in April of aiding the Islamic State Khorasan, or ISIS-K, the terrorist group that claimed responsibility for the bombing. The attack at Afghanistan’s main airport killed 13 American troops and more than 150 Afghans, and became a symbol of the chaotic U.S. withdrawal from the country during the opening months of the Biden administration.

But jurors could not decide whether Mr. Sharifullah should be held directly responsible for the airport attack.

The bombing took place at what was known as Abbey Gate, the entry point to Hamid Karzai International Airport in Kabul, the capital. It had become a gathering point for thousands of civilians who were seeking to flee Afghanistan as the Taliban took hold of the country.

Mr. Sharifullah, who was arrested in Pakistan last year, was accused of helping a suicide bomber reach the airport without being detected. The bomber walked into a crowd of civilians at Abbey Gate and detonated an explosive hidden under his clothing.

“Mohammad Sharifullah has dedicated his life to violence and murder for the sake of hatred,” Theophani K. Stamos, a deputy to the U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, said in a statement on Wednesday. “We cannot restore the lives he has taken, but we can bring a measure of justice to the families who lost so much on that day.”

Mr. Sharifullah faced the possibility of life in prison. The jury in his trial unanimously agreed that he was a member of ISIS-K and convicted him of conspiracy to provide material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization. They split on whether there was enough evidence to blame him for the Abbey Gate attack.

Lawyers for Mr. Sharifullah argued during his trial that he was not responsible for the attack.

Geremy Kamens, a lawyer for Mr. Sharifullah, said in an email on Thursday that hearing from families of some of the service members during Mr. Sharifullah’s sentencing on Wednesday was “heartbreaking.”

“Those families deserve to see the people responsible for that attack brought to justice,” he wrote. “But the jury heard the evidence and did not find that Mr. Sharifullah was among them.”

After Mr. Sharifullah was transferred to U.S. custody, the F.B.I. said he told agents that he was a member of ISIS-K and that he knew the operative who blew himself up at Abbey Gate. He also admitted to scouting the attacker’s route to the airport, the agency said.

Mr. Sharifullah’s defense lawyer, however, disavowed his confession, saying it was false and coerced.

The prosecution’s case relied heavily on the confession. During the trial, the judge instructed the jury that they could not convict based on a confession if it was not corroborated by other evidence.

The F.B.I. said Mr. Sharifullah had admitted to having played a part in other ISIS-K terrorist attacks: He provided transportation for the bomber accused of a 2016 suicide attack on the Canadian Embassy in Kabul, which killed at least 10 people. The bureau also linked him to an attack on a music venue in Moscow in 2024 that killed about 130 people. He also admitted to sharing instructions on how to use assault rifles with two of the four gunman who were charged in the Moscow attack, the F.B.I. said.

Overall, prosecutors said, Mr. Sharifullah participated in more than a dozen attacks over nearly a decade.

item.title: E.U.-Canada Ambitions Face Reality Check
item.description:
The European Union’s invitation Wednesday for Canada to become an “associate member” of the bloc shows just how intent these traditional United States allies are on pursuing a more stable future by binding closer together.

“We must urgently reimagine our partnerships,” Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, said in the European Parliament in Strasbourg, a beaming Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada sitting just to her side. But there are no guarantees they will get there.

While details of what this relationship might look like remain scant, Ms. von der Leyen noted some potential areas of cooperation, including partnerships in manufacturing, technology, defense, energy policy and economic security.

This would not be “a partnership against anyone else,” she insisted, “but for our common strength.”

European officials said that, in the lead-up to the speech on Wednesday, the bloc wanted to ensure that President Trump did not see this new partnership with Canada as an anti-American move.

Still, if it isn’t precisely against the United States, then it’s unmistakably about it.

“Behind this is a desire to hedge against what for both partners is an increasingly fraught relationship with the United States,” said Ian Lesser, a distinguished fellow of the German Marshall Fund, based in Brussels.

“But it’s not just that it’s fraught,” he added. “It’s the most important geoeconomic and geopolitical relationship for both Europe and for Canada.”

For Mr. Carney, the invitation is both timely and symbolically important. He has decided to stand up to Mr. Trump, who has imposed tariffs on Canada and regularly threatens its sovereignty.

Mr. Carney has been pushing for Canada to get greater access to the European Union — its territory, its market, its funds and programs — without becoming a full member of the bloc.

He has found an enthusiastic partner in Ms. von der Leyen, who has painted Canada as a dependable source for Europe’s needs for energy and critical raw materials, as well as a steadfast ally who shares NATO membership, support for Ukraine and a commitment to the rule of law. Ms. von der Leyen does not represent the European Union’s 27 countries, but she sets the agenda for the bloc and commands its mighty bureaucracy.

The tie-up seems to make sense at a moment of global turbulence and a shifting global role for the United States. Between them, the European Union’s 27 members and Canada have more than 490 million citizens and include four of the world’s 10 largest economies.

The European Union is underpinned by dense, deep legal and procedural rules, built over decades by a group of nations that ceded sovereignty to one another, and to an unelected executive branch in Brussels.

Inserting a country an ocean away deeper into this web is not a straightforward business.

The label the European Union wants to confer on Canada, “associate member,” is not an existing type of partnership — meaning that it is not clear what actions Canada would have to take to earn it, or for it to be given.

“It has no legal basis,” said Mujtaba Rahman, managing director for Europe at the Eurasia Group. “It’s more symbolism and signal,” he added.

Ms. von der Leyen was taking a risk using the term, which had been floating for weeks ahead of her speech, and drew consternation from several member states, according to European officials.

It is seen as vague, untethered from legal frameworks and potentially antagonistic toward countries that already have detailed legal agreements with the European Union. These range from candidate nations such as Albania to close partners including Britain, Switzerland and Norway. Those countries have deep trade ties to the bloc and, in the case of Switzerland and Norway, have free movement into and out of other European nations.

Some Canadian officials do not appear to love the term, either, as membership in the European Union implies forfeiting some sovereignty, which is the opposite of what Mr. Carney has pledged to do. The Conservative opposition leader seized on the term, arguing that if Canada was never to be the 51st state of the United States, it should also not become the 28th member state of the European Union.

“There’s a lot of good will, but once one starts to look just a little bit closer, one also finds that many Europeans really don’t know Canada all that well, and they maybe aren’t fully taking on board Canada’s own sensitivities to sovereignty,” said Mr. Lesser.

Hours after Ms. von der Leyen spoke on Wednesday, the incoming Canadian ambassador to the European Union said that labels did not matter — but suggested that Canada preferred “alliance for the future” to describe the emerging new bond with the European Union. That phrase also appeared in Ms. von der Leyen’s speech.

“I think we’re still a ways away from actually landing on what we think the best way to describe it is,” said Jonathan Wilkinson.

Three European diplomats said that the title “associate member” may not stick.

Officials from both sides are working to find tangible progress that they hope to announce at a European Union-Canada summit scheduled to take place in Montreal at the end of October.

Two officials, one from the European Union and one from Canada, with knowledge of the talks, said that officials were trying hard to reach that goal, but that work had been slow and difficult, in part because it is highly technical.

Just how hard it can be to get the European Union to agree on anything has been displayed frequently over the years. For example, talks over a trade agreement with Mercosur, the South American bloc, lasted a quarter century.

Canada has its own experience with these E.U. rigidities — and has some of its own. Its free-trade agreement with the bloc, in effect in practice for a decade, has still not been ratified by 10 of the 27 member states, for various reasons.

Canada already participates in a handful of E.U. ventures, including Horizon, a technology and innovation research effort, and SAFE, a defense industrial program. It had to pay $100 million to participate in Horizon, and participation in other E.U. programs is also likely to require Canada to pay into a budget.

One more immediate benefit for Canada from closer ties to Europe may be in securing funding from the European Investment Bank. The major development bank, which is owned by the E.U. member states and has more than $630 billion in assets, is eager and ready to invest in Canadian projects, particularly in critical raw materials, and its leader is heading to Ottawa on Sunday to advance talks with the Canadian government.

The bank is ready to start work in Canada, a European official with knowledge of the preparations said, but needed Ottawa to approve certain administrative formalities such as allowing E.U. diplomats to work there.

Some of the ideas being discussed ahead of the October summit show the ambitious scope of the Canada-E.U. future relationship.

For example, officials said, Mr. Carney wants the bloc to work with Canada to build systems for payments and cloud computing that will offer an alternative to those of the United States in a bid to secure sovereignty.

Discussions have also been underway on a digital trade agreement, which could deepen cooperation on cybersecurity and regulatory cooperation.

Talks are more advanced to bring Canadian regulations in line with European ones in energy, including the monitoring, reporting and evaluation system used by the bloc to track methane emissions from vessels fueled by liquefied natural gas, as well as gas imports entering the European Union market. This is a necessity if Canada is going to export gas to the European Union.

Another area where Canada is particularly eager to see movement is the ability of its citizens to spend longer stretches of time in the European Union visa-free, have their professional qualifications recognized there and be able to study in European universities.

Because these policy areas hinge on complex and politically fraught immigration rules, major breakthroughs could be difficult. Additionally, any agreement improving Canadians’ access to Europe would require reciprocity, meaning that it would grant the same access to Canada for 450 million Europeans.

Some European diplomats have suggested that Erasmus — Europe’s popular student exchange program — could be an easier starting place for collaboration.

item.title: The Hidden Human Cost of Kim Jong-un’s New Power
item.description:
His nation is now a de facto nuclear power. Its economy is growing at the fastest pace in years. He has been courted by the leaders of China, Russia and the United States.

Kim Jong-un, the North Korean dictator, has emerged as an unlikely winner of the post-pandemic era. And his newfound strength rests on the systematic exploitation of his own people, which is actively facilitated by Moscow and Beijing.

By supplying troops and ammunition for Russia’s war in Ukraine, Mr. Kim is estimated to be reaping billions of dollars. Russia is repaying Pyongyang in advanced military technology and critical commodities like flour, pork and oil — goods his regime can then resell at home for profit.

But the human cost is staggering, for North Koreans at home and abroad.

Thousands of North Korean soldiers have been killed or wounded on faraway battlefields.

“I tremble as I await the daily reports, wondering how many soldiers were lost, whether they suffered reckless losses in the pursuit of bravery, whether they succumbed to fear or fell captive to the enemy,” one young North Korean platoon leader wrote in his diary before he, too, died in combat.

Thousands more North Koreans toil behind the front lines, working in military drone factories, repairing war-damaged cities and building apartments across Russia to meet revenue quotas set by Mr. Kim’s government. With Moscow looking the other way to evade sanctions, many enter Russia on student visas but never see a classroom — instead sleeping in shipping containers and enduring 14-hour shifts with hardly any days off.

Closer to home, China is openly importing North Korean coal in violation of United Nations sanctions, satellite imagery indicates. Defectors say the commodity is mined by workers trapped in forced labor in central and northern North Korea.

Even North Korea’s biggest official export — hair products like wigs and false eyelashes, which are not subject to U.N. penalties — has brutal origins. Much of that merchandise is produced in labor camps, where inmates are forced to meet daily quotas and, survivors say, risk starvation if they fail. The payoff for Pyongyang was $188 million in sales to China in 2024 alone, according to Chinese customs data.

On paper, North Korea is a socialist state, with free provisions for citizens. In reality, it is a regime of quotas, in which everyone must contribute to a shadow economy that sustains Mr. Kim’s extravagant lifestyle and military ambitions — lavish dinners, armored cars, luxury yachts, seaside resorts and nuclear missiles.

“North Korea claims to be a tax-free country where everything is free,” said Ryu Hyeon-woo, who was its acting ambassador to Kuwait when he defected. “In reality, its system survives by milking its people.”

North Korea’s economy has grown more than 3 percent in each of the past three years, according to South Korea’s central bank, a drastic reversal from its pandemic-era contraction. To uncover the methods driving this turnaround, The New York Times spoke with dozens of North Korean defectors, human rights investigators and geopolitical analysts.

The first thing that Baek Hye-ok said she noticed at the Chongori labor camp in northeast North Korea was the smell.

A cell no larger than a two-car garage held more than 100 women. Wardens, unable to bear the stench of unwashed bodies, ordered inmates to kneel 10 feet away when summoned. Bedbugs dropped into bowls of gruel.

“You didn’t spit it out because your life depended on it,” Ms. Baek recalled years later in Seoul. “You never forget the stomach-churning smell when a bedbug bursts between your teeth.”

Work began at dawn. Young women with sharp eyesight stitched wigs and false eyelashes. Trucks delivered raw materials labeled in Chinese and departed with finished goods. Prison officials told inmates that the shipments went to China through the nearby city of Rason, Ms. Baek said.

“Your life depended on meeting your quota,” she said. “Fail, and you were beaten and your ration cut.”

During separate interviews, Ms. Baek and Lee Young-ju, another former inmate who defected and now lives in Seoul, said that roughly one in every 10 inmates died each year. They were quickly replaced by new arrivals — many of whom had been caught foraging for food across the border in China because they did not have enough to eat at home. Others were being punished for watching smuggled South Korean dramas. Some inmates were so desperate that they ate maggots from corpses. Ms. Lee spent three years at the labor camp while Ms. Baek put in two years over two stints.

“The place was a living hell,” Ms. Lee said.

Few can escape quotas, defectors say.

Villagers scour hills for berries bound for China. Schoolchildren supply rabbit hides for soldiers’ gloves. Tractor plants run dual lines: farm machinery on one, tanks on the other. Elites fund gold-plated statues of Mr. Kim’s father and grandfather, and maintain the Pyongyang mausoleum where their embalmed bodies lie. The 1.3-million-strong army — the world’s fourth largest — doubles as a free work force, dispatched to construction sites.

The scramble for revenue extends abroad.

Diplomats smuggle Cuban cigars and African rhino horns inside diplomatic pouches to raise “loyalty funds” for Mr. Kim, or to feed his family’s taste for Russian king crab, Arabian sweets and gold-tipped Montblanc pens, said Mr. Ryu, a son-in-law of the former head of the ruling Workers’ Party’s Bureau 39, which manages Mr. Kim’s secret funds.

Even the General Bureau of Reconnaissance — North Korea’s main intelligence agency — moonlights as a business. At one point, it ran restaurants and a squad of 19 hackers and IT workers out of the United Arab Emirates, Mr. Ryu said. They stole cryptocurrency or used stolen identities to take freelance coding jobs.

Pyongyang selects young students gifted in math and science, training them from an early age to become software engineers or hackers. It later deploys them to China, Russia and the Middle East, where they help fill the regime’s coffers while living in dormitories and being monitored by secret police. In the first four months of this year alone, they accounted for 76 percent of all cryptocurrency stolen worldwide, according to TRM Labs, an analytics company.

Mr. Ryu said a North Korean banking operative named Sim Hyon Sop had been central to laundering the earnings of these workers in the Middle East. The U.A.E.-based money-laundering network run by Mr. Sim and his Chinese partners has also been cited in U.S. court documents and a Treasury Department sanctions report.

Son Myong-hwa’s father labored underground in iron ore mines until lung disease claimed his life at 59. He spent days on end in the suffocating darkness of the pit, especially when the authorities raised production quotas. When Ms. Son arrived with lunchboxes, he and his co-workers were so caked in dust that “only their eyes and teeth flashed white when they smiled,” she said.

Mines serve as a dumping ground for those deemed lowest-class, including South Korean prisoners of war from the 1950s and their descendants — among them Ms. Son’s father and siblings.

Jeong Sun-nam, whose father and siblings worked mostly in iron ore mines, said her father survived three underground explosion accidents. When blasts shattered the shafts, she recalled, the miners’ wives clawed at the rubble with bare hands until their fingers bled.

“Minerals from North Korea are stained with blood,” said Ms. Jeong, who, like Ms. Son, managed to defect to South Korea.

Coal and iron-ore exports have long been an economic lifeline, though U.N. sanctions began squeezing the trade about a decade ago. Yet, smuggling has thrived, with ships cutting their tracking transponders and swapping illicit cargo in the open ocean. Satellite imagery analyzed last year by the London-based Open Source Center identified six repeat offenders ferrying North Korean coal and iron ore to Chinese ports.

Now even the pretense of secrecy is vanishing, especially after Russia and China dismantled in 2024 the U.N. panel monitoring sanctions enforcement.

A July report by the Citizens’ Alliance for North Korean Human Rights, a nonprofit based in Seoul, found that visits by large cargo ships to Nampo, North Korea’s primary coal and oil terminal, had surged fivefold since 2019. Blacklisted vessels no longer hide in the shadows — instead, the report said, they dock “openly” at Chinese terminals.

Lee Eun-pyong was a sergeant in North Korea’s 131st Guidance Bureau — the agency responsible for construction, security and uranium mining for North Korea’s nuclear program. In 2017 he was ordered to go to Russia and earn money for the regime. He said he and 33 of his comrades were heralded as “forefront warriors of the country’s nuclear power buildup.”

Their days in Moscow began at 7 a.m. and stretched past midnight, he said. The men slept on the dusty floors of unfinished buildings or crammed into shipping containers, chasing a mandatory monthly income quota of $600. On paper, he was enrolled at the European Institute Justo, a university in Moscow, but he was put to work laying bricks, making concrete slabs and plastering walls.

“We didn’t even know where the school was,” he recalled, after defecting to South Korea.

Under Mr. Kim, exporting laborers has become nearly every state agency’s side hustle. An estimated 100,000 North Korean workers remain in China, defying a 2019 U.N. repatriation deadline. Russia issued more than 36,000 entry visas to North Koreans last year — a fourfold jump from 2024 — nearly all for education, according to Russian government data. The Citizens’ Alliance and the Database Center for North Korean Human Rights, another nonprofit in Seoul, say that Pyongyang conspired with Russian schools like Sodeistvie College in Moscow to disguise workers’ labor in construction sites and sewing and meat-processing factories as “internships” and their wages as “scholarships.”

Today, Russian staffing agencies openly advertise North Korean workers for long shifts at textile mills, restaurants and farms. Job postings actively seek Korean interpreters. One Russian mayor said that demand for North Korean laborers — who “work like robots”— was so high that his city couldn’t afford them as street sweepers.

“We guarantee discipline: Employees work strictly according to the schedule, without smoke breaks or absences,” one staffing agency’s pitch reads. Another Moscow-area listing offered 40 North Korean women for hire, insisting that any future employer house them together — a condition their North Korean supervisors demand to prevent defections.

An investigation by the Dutch nonprofit Global Rights Compliance found that North Korean workers in Russia average 14-hour days, with some receiving only two days off a year. They live under the suffocating watch of security officers sent from Pyongyang. Three former workers, interviewed separately by The Times, recalled that the deepest sting was watching co-workers from Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia call their families freely while they could not.

To survive, the North Koreans dug through dumpsters for discarded clothes, they said. When one worker was sent home, others pressed letters into his hands for their families, with whatever money they had saved — usually a $20 bill — tucked inside. (The U.S. dollar is the most coveted currency in North Korea.)

During the pandemic, Pyongyang raised quotas and ordered laborers in Russia to keep working, citing the state’s own economic strain, according to a North Korean worker who fled Russia for South Korea in 2022. One man, he said, was escorted outside his work sites exactly once in five years — to buy gifts for his family the day before he finally went home.

“We were nothing but draft animals,” said the worker, who asked to be identified only by his last name, Han.

Last year, Ukrainian troops found a dead North Korean officer in Russia’s Kursk region. Documents recovered from his body exposed the predicament facing the estimated 16,000 North Korean troops Mr. Kim has dispatched to Russia — they were, essentially, cannon fodder. South Korean intelligence estimates that as many as 2,000 have been killed.

The documents — obtained by the Human Rights Foundation, a New York-based nonprofit — listed deployment plans, instructions and battlefield experiences of North Korean troops. A two-page document noted that some North Korean troops faced “a barrage of enemy artillery fire and suicide drones swarming in like a cloud of hornets.” When soldiers fell, their comrades often rushed to rescue them, disregarding enemy fire and suffering further casualties. Russian evacuation vehicles routinely took more than 10 hours to reach the wounded.

“Because of the failure to evacuate the wounded in time,” one document stated, “combatants were sacrificed during the evacuation.”

The account stands in stark contrast to the official narrative in North Korea, which glorifies the fallen as martyrs and claims that many had chosen to detonate hand grenades rather than risk capture while wounded.

The diary of the fallen platoon leader revealed the human cost of that pressure. Ukrainian special forces recovered the diary from the dead soldier and shared it with the Human Rights Foundation, where it was reviewed by a staff member who was a North Korean defector. In its pages, the officer alluded to his struggle between the duty to demonstrate “unparalleled bravery in battles” for “the greatest joy and satisfaction to the homeland and the party,” and a private fear that his ambition would ultimately cost his men their lives.

In December 2024, he wrote a final prayer for his fallen comrades. That same month, he wrote to his “princess” back home, leaving behind a promise in case he did not return.

If he died, he wrote, “I will become a butterfly and find you.”

item.title: A New Play in Budapest Signals a Cultural Reawakening for Hungary
item.description:
When she returned in 1989 to the homeland that her family fled after Soviet troops crushed an uprising in 1956, Kati Marton was “filled with great hope” as she watched a “young, skinny bearded guy” shout for Soviet withdrawal.

Then, after she started making annual trips to Budapest, the Hungarian capital and place of her birth, Ms. Marton, a Hungarian-American writer, watched aghast as Viktor Orban, no longer young or skinny but Hungary’s strongman leader, cozied up to the Kremlin and championed what he called “illiberal democracy.”

Media outlets he controlled began denouncing her as a subversive who was plotting to overthrow his government in cahoots with George Soros, the Hungarian-born financier and liberal philanthropist. So she halted her visits home.

After Mr. Orban’s crushing defeat in an April election, Ms. Marton recently returned for her first trip back in eight years to attend the Hungarian premiere of a one-woman play based on her 2009 family memoir, “Enemies of the People.”

The play, also called “Enemies of the People,” about the perils of authoritarianism, might have been staged not at all, or with some risk, were Mr. Orban still in power. Its opening, now that his once seemingly invincible Fidesz party has lost heavily, is being celebrated by the former government’s opponents as a sign of changing times.

It features Erika Marozsan, a prominent Hungarian film and stage actress, playing Ms. Marton as she recounts the ordeals, hidden histories (including their Jewish roots) and infidelities of her parents in postwar Budapest, accompanied by a violinist and accordion player.

Both parents worked as journalists reporting on Stalinist show trials for American wire services, the AP and UPI. They played bridge with American diplomats and cruised around town in a white Studebaker convertible, and they were arrested in 1955, branded enemies of the state and convicted of espionage.

Released amid a brief retreat from hard-line Stalinism, they fled with their two young daughters, Kati and her older sister, Julia, to the United States in 1957 after Soviet troops stomped out an anti-Communist uprising.

Hungary’s recent election, Ms. Marton said, “wasn’t an uprising” but was still “splendid proof that Hungarians were unbowed and that you can only push them so far. They said: ‘No, enough, we don’t want this anymore.’”

The English-language play about her family was performed at the Central European University, a bastion of liberal thinking in Budapest that, like Ms. Marton and much of Hungary’s intelligentsia, is now rejoicing at Mr. Orban’s departure.

Founded in 1991 by Mr. Soros to “promote the values of open society — including free expression and diversity of beliefs,” the university was stripped of its right to issue degrees by a law passed under Mr. Orban in 2017 and relocated most of its teaching to Vienna.

Mathias Moschel, the university’s vice rector, said there were no immediate plans to move students back to Budapest but added that a partial return may be possible now that Mr. Orban, who was prime minister for 20 years in all, had been sidelined.

“All of a sudden, there is a different reality in Hungary, and it is wonderful,” Mr. Moschel said in an interview. Mr. Orban’s ouster, he added, “removed a sword of Damocles hanging over all our heads. You never knew when or if it would fall.”

Not everyone, of course, is celebrating. Hardcore fans of Mr. Orban are in a deep funk as the people they reviled before the election as “woke globalists” and traitorous “Soros agents” return to the fore.

Mr. Orban, passive and mostly silent after his defeat, announced over the weekend that the time had come “to take off the gloves and fight.”

For the moment, however, the “new reality” seems secure, and Hungarians glad to see the back of Mr. Orban are exultant.

“People are smiling again,” said Krisztina Bezi, a schoolteacher who attended the recent premiere in the university auditorium. The play, she said, “would not have happened under Orban.”

Flora Laszlo, the head of the Central European University’s culture unit, said the play could perhaps have been performed before the election but only after careful review of the possible consequences. “We always had to pay attention to the events we organized and the government’s attitude,” she said.

Ms. Marton, addressing the packed auditorium after the show, feted what she called her “second homecoming,” rejoicing that Hungary is now “on the right side of history.”

She had stayed away from her homeland, she explained in an interview, not because she thought she would be arrested but because she wanted to avoid any “risk of harassment, provocation or other unpleasantness” of the kind that often befell people Mr. Orban viewed as enemies.

Among the first acts of the new government was the abolition in June of the Sovereignty Protection Office, a state agency set up in 2023 to investigate people and organizations deemed to be serving foreign interests. The agency had turned its sights on Ms. Marton and several of her associates after an elaborate dirty tricks operation in 2024 targeting Hungarians with ties to a New York-based group, Action for Democracy.

“Like most autocrats or would-be autocrats, Orban needed demons, a constant supply of them, and toward the end I became one,” Ms. Marton said.

For Mr. Orban’s foes, the show’s opening signaled the end of Hungary’s long detour from the European path that was first staked out with the collapse of Communism in 1989.

Attila Punyi, an economist in the audience, said it “feels great to be back in Europe” after years of increasingly close ties between Budapest and Moscow. “I can’t describe how happy we are.”

Ms. Marozsan, the actress, said the play had been conceived before the April election as “an act of rebellion” against Mr. Orban’s seemingly immovable system and as a warning of where he might take Hungary next.

She said she “cried for a day with joy” after Mr. Orban had lost. But she cautioned that Hungary’s new prime minister, Peter Magyar, a onetime Orban ally who is himself a conservative, was unlikely to swiftly satisfy the hopes of Mr. Orban’s many critics in Budapest. “Everything is not going to change overnight so we have to wait and be patient again,” she said.

The mayor of Budapest, Gergely Karacsony, a longstanding liberal standard-bearer, attended the show and said he liked its message. But he lamented that Mr. Magyar had so far done nothing to relieve his city’s financial troubles, which, he said, where exacerbated by the previous government’s hostility toward Hungary’s liberal capital.

Janos Mohacsi, a veteran Hungarian director who wrote the script for the play with his brother, Istvan, said Orban loyalists responsible for his dismissal from teaching and theater jobs still dominated major cultural institutions, including the national theater. “I’m not a vengeful person,” he said, “but they should leave.”

Hungary under Mr. Orban, Mr. Mohacsi said, “was not a police state” but a “mafia state” and it will take years to uproot entrenched networks in the arts, the media, the judiciary and other arms of officialdom. But, he added, “every parallel between this play about the 1950s and our contemporary reality ended with the election.”

item.title: Carney Calls for E.U.-Canada Pact Amid ‘Ferocious Storm’
item.description:
Canada’s newly proposed associate membership in the European Union will help secure sovereignty and freedom for the country amid a “ferocious storm,” Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada told the European Parliament on Thursday.

Mr. Carney said that the broad alliance outlined by a top E.U. leader on Wednesday would strengthen core areas of life on both sides of the Atlantic, and shield Europeans and Canadians from being dominated.

But, he said, Canada and the European Union were not looking to become another superpower.

“I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival only with better manners,” he said, speaking at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France. “We do not seek power to dominate others.”

The announcement that Canada and the European Union were beginning negotiations for a unique kind of alliance, the closest the bloc of 27 nations would have with any nonmember state, highlighted the deep desire for the traditional allies of the United States to seek stability and prosperity together as President Trump remakes the American role in the world.

On Wednesday, Mr. Trump threatened to punish the European Union for offering such a deep connection with Canada, calling it a “hostile” act.

Mr. Carney suggested that Europe and Canada were seeking to band together only “so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”

Mr. Trump has instigated a trade war against Canada, the United States’ closest ally and second-largest trading partner, and routinely said that he wanted the northern neighbor to become the 51st state. He has also pulled the United States away from the traditional close alliance with the European Union, imposing tariffs and barriers to trade, and weakening the NATO defense pact by threatening to drastically cut the American contribution even as Russia’s war in Ukraine rages on.

Canada and the European Union will work to deepen their link through treaties and joint policies in a vast range of policies, Mr. Carney said. He proposed, for example, that youth from both Canada and the bloc be able to travel and study in each other’s territories through participation in the European Union student-mobility program, Erasmus. That program is credited with building generations of young Europeans with joint identities and experiences.

Mr. Carney’s vision for how the European Union and Canada can work together also extended to major, foundational parts of their economies and society. He said the two should launch a “deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities,” including industries involving critical minerals, defense, A.I. and computing capabilities, and energy security. He also suggested the bloc and Canada could work on managing payments systems.

The question of who controls the data and core infrastructure for aspects of daily life like payments systems has been worrying policymakers in the European Union and Canada, whose societies are dependent on systems controlled by the United States or by American companies. That concern is front and center as the debate grows about the future of artificial intelligence.

“Canada and Europe can join forces to develop A.I. safety protocols, coordinate common standards and strengthen transparency, while developing applications so our governments and companies can serve our citizens better,” Mr. Carney said.

He added that Canada is endowed with major critical mineral and energy resources, which the country wants to export to markets in the European Union. The two already have agreements in place for such collaboration. Earlier this year, Canada secured a major contract to sell liquefied natural gas to Germany.

Mr. Carney, who made extensive references to the deep bonds between Europe and Canada through their joint history and experience fighting side-by-side in wars, framed this new cooperation as existential.

“Freedom and life must be earned every single day,” he said. “Every day. Not once in 1945, or 1956, or 1989. Every day, including this one.”

item.title: Trump’s Economic Vise Leaves Cubans Desperate for Food and Medicine
item.description:
Thousands of containers filled with food, medicine and other goods bound for Cuba have been stranded throughout the Caribbean since two shipping giants stopped deliveries to avoid tough U.S. sanctions, according to diplomats, Cuban officials, merchants and others involved in the imports.

The containers stranded in various ports include humanitarian aid, from solar panels to medication to colostomy bags. Dozens of containers of aid purchased by different United Nations agencies are among them.

U.S. sanctions have also hobbled shipments by air, and forced the World Health Organization to scrap planned deliveries of cancer drugs.

The challenges of delivering vital materials have sharply aggravated longstanding shortages, added to an enormous backlog of patients awaiting surgery and sent grocery prices soaring as Cubans live through the island’s worst humanitarian crisis since the 1959 revolution. With food becoming prohibitively expensive, hunger is rising and soup kitchens are struggling to fill the gap.

The Trump administration has imposed an economic vise on Cuba and its ruling communist party to try to force political and economic change.

In January, the administration imposed an oil blockade on the island. Then in May, it cranked up the pressure by announcing that foreign companies working with certain Cuban state entities risked having their assets frozen and being locked out of doing business with U.S. companies and banks.

Shortly after, Hapag-Lloyd, a German shipping company, and CMA CGM, a French one — which experts say together delivered at least half of Cuba’s imports, including most of its food — quit delivering to the island.

The development adds another layer of misery for Cubans already struggling under daily blackouts, fuel and food shortages and a collapsing health system. It also puts more pressure on the Cuban government as it tries to survive the Trump administration’s pressure campaign.

Dr. Valia Rodríguez, a Cuban doctor in Britain who runs a charity called Aid for the Caribbean, said a Hapag-Lloyd container her organization filled with more than $500,000 worth of resuscitation kits, colostomy bags and intravenous tubes left Northern Ireland in April. It arrived at the Port of Mariel in Cuba on June 4, a day before the new sanctions aimed at foreign companies went into full effect.

“They decided to stop unloading the containers,” said Dr. Rodríguez, referring to Hapag-Lloyd.

The containers were instead sent to Panama, where the charity says it has had to pay more than $6,000 in storage fees, as patients who have had colon surgery turn to desperate measures. “Right now, people in Cuba are using shopping bags, because there are no colostomy bags,” Dr. Rodríguez said.

Spare parts from a dismantled power plant in Uruguay, donated to Cuba by the South American nation’s state-owned power company, have been unable to leave because no shipping line will take them to the island, according to diplomats. Cuba has suffered at least five nationwide blackouts this year as its aging power grid repeatedly collapses.

Though the U.S. government has explicitly stated that its sanctions are not intended to prohibit the delivery of food and medical supplies, Francisco Pichón, the U.N. coordinator in Cuba who runs its humanitarian response, said sanctions were jamming up the organization’s relief effort because shippers were wary of taking any chances.

“We are facing something very real, which is a phenomenon called ‘overcompliance,’” Mr. Pichón said. “Overcompliance is a really excessive precaution from companies to not expose themselves to sanctions.”

As of last week, the U.N. humanitarian relief effort was still awaiting delivery of 30 containers holding water treatment kits, antibiotics, contraceptives and pregnancy tests.

A lack of jet fuel has also decimated air traffic to Cuba, shutting off another cargo delivery route.

Despite months of attempts, thousands of donated vials of a cancer drug called doxorubicin failed to reach the island after several airlines stopped flying to Cuba, according to the Pan American Health Organization.

The World Health Organization said tuberculosis medication it purchased from an Indian pharmaceutical firm meant to leave by air via D.H.L. was returned to the manufacturer in May without explanation. Other humanitarian aid shipments had to be airlifted on special charter flights, U.N. agencies said.

Businesses have considered routing their cargo through the United States because shipments are still coming from there. But the cost of the extra shipping more than doubled the price of cheaper products like rice, making much of it too expensive to sell in Cuba, a person involved in Cuba business trade said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to protect business operations.

Business owners have been debating whether to abandon their cargo in foreign ports, the person said.

The State Department, has said that sanctions hold the “corrupt” Cuban regime and its financial backers to account, including GAESA, the military conglomerate that controls large parts of the island’s economy.

In a statement to The New York Times, the State Department said the government’s “blatant kleptocracy” and its economic mismanagement directed scarce resources for the benefit of officials, the military and the intelligence apparatus rather than the Cuban people.

“Our tough Cuba policy restricts financial transactions with entities owned or controlled by Cuban security services in order to cut the regime off from resources used to line its pockets and violently oppress the Cuban people,” the statement said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters in September that “if Cuba is a humanitarian disaster, it is because their regime is a disaster, because the economic model they follow doesn’t work.”

Rodolfo Benítez Verson, Cuba’s ambassador to the United Nations in Geneva, told the U.N. Human Rights Council last week that more than 7,000 containers bound for Cuba were stranded.

“The cruelty knows no bounds,” Mr. Benítez said. “They will have to answer to the Cuban people, and they will not be forgiven.”

Hapag-Lloyd, the German shipping line, said in a statement that it had made a “business decision” not to continue the Cuba maritime route and that it was working toward a “swift and practical solution” for the cargo.

CMA CGM, the French company, said in a statement that it had resumed limited services of “compliant cargo” to the island, such as agricultural products, medicines and medical devices.

Given the scale of the backlog it would take months for all the containers to reach the island, businesspeople, diplomats and humanitarian workers said.

The People’s Forum, a left-wing organization based in New York, said it had three containers stranded with roughly 1,000 solar panels costing over $750,000 meant to power hospital intensive care units. Purchased in Mexico, they are now stuck there, said Manolo De Los Santos, an organizer with the group.

“The bigger thing for us is the anguish of knowing there are literally surgical rooms without electricity and 100,000 patients waiting for surgeries,” he said.

The Cuban government, in a new report detailing the effects of the U.S. oil blockade, said 100,000 patients were awaiting operations, including 12,000 children.

With few viable commercial shipping routes available, exports to Cuba have plummeted.

Brazilian and Mexican exports to Cuba were both down over 90 percent in July compared with the same month last year, according to Brazilian and Mexican government official statistics.

“Up to two-thirds of the overall container shipping capacity has disappeared,” said Gordon Wilmsmeier, a professor of shipping and global logistics at Universidad de los Andes in Colombia.

It has become so difficult to ship supplies to Cuba that some sympathetic nations have turned to their militaries. Mexico, which stopped shipping oil to Cuba in January after President Trump threatened tariffs, used Navy ships to deliver items like thousands of tons of rice and beans, as well as bags of powdered milk. The Brazilian Air Force flew in shipments of powdered milk.

Celso Amorim, a top foreign policy adviser to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil, said in an interview that Brazil would like to provide Cuba with fuel and more aid, but is wary of Washington’s reaction.

“This is part of the reality of the present world,” he said. “It’s complicated. Every company here — even state companies or quasi-state companies — have interests in the United States, and they are afraid of being affected.”

At markets in Havana, the price of frozen chicken has doubled in recent months, while the price of a carton of 30 eggs has tripled to $11 — higher than the average monthly salary.

Food prices increased 60 percent from January to August, according to Omar Everleny Pérez Villanueva, a Cuban economist.

Soup kitchens have proliferated in Havana, the capital, but are running short of goods.

Quisicuaba, a state-linked religious nonprofit that, said it was waiting for five food containers. The quantity of chicken and eggs has dwindled, said Luis Enrique Alemán, who is in charge of Quisicuaba’s kitchen supplies.

“Such a drastic reduction in supplies forces us to work miracles and rethink our recipes,” he said.

Amid hundreds of people waiting to fill plastic tubs with food, Carmen Carballo García, 66, sat on a bench while her 5-year-old granddaughter, Yaquelin, sucked her thumb.

“The doctors tell me she is underweight,” Ms. Carballo said. “She needs milk, but she doesn’t have any.”

Jack Nicas contributed reporting from Brasília.
